\chapter{Hablan --- They, and Ustedes}
\label{ch:spanish-hablan}
\hlchaptermodality{38}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what they do, and address any group as ustedes.}

ustedes is vuestras mercedes - so it takes the they form for the same reason usted takes the he form.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hablan]{hablan — \textquotedblleft{}they speak,\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}you all speak\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C07-hablan}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}we speak.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Hablamos}.) And what was the form for \emph{he speaks}? (\emph{Habla}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: add the plural -n}]
Take \emph{habla}, the form for one other person, and add \textbf{-n}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{hablan} — \emph{they speak.}
\end{quote}

That is the whole operation, and it is the same one Spanish uses everywhere: a final \textbf{-n} on a verb means the subject is plural and is not you.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the form does a second job, exactly as habla did}]
\textbf{ustedes} — \emph{you all}. And it takes \textbf{hablan}, the \emph{they} form.

You have seen this exact move before. \emph{Usted} takes the \emph{he/she} form because it grew out of \emph{vuestra merced}, \textquotedblleft{}your grace\textquotedblright{} — a thing you talk \textbf{about}. \textbf{Ustedes} is simply that phrase made plural, \emph{vuestras mercedes}, \textquotedblleft{}your graces\textquotedblright{}. Same origin, same consequence.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Where this is the ordinary word.} Across all of Latin America, and in the Canary Islands and parts of Andalusia, \textbf{ustedes} is how you address \emph{any} group — friends, family, strangers alike. There is no separate familiar plural. For most Spanish speakers alive, this lesson is the complete answer to \textquotedblleft{}how do I talk to more than one person?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Spain uses a different word for friends, and it has the next chapter to itself.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}habla\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}hablan\textquotedblright{} — one other person, then several
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ustedes hablan\textquotedblright{}, addressing a group you have just met
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}they speak\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Hablan}.) What does a final \textbf{-n} on a verb tell you? (The subject is \textbf{plural}, and not you.) And who does \emph{ustedes} address in Latin America? (\textbf{Any} group at all.) Next: the word Spain uses instead, for friends.
\end{tcolorbox}
